title: Dependent columns: many best fits
summary: When one column is a multiple of another, a whole line of fits is equally good.

blocks.title: All three x are 2

define.meaning: One column is a combination of the others. Here column 2 is $2 \times$ column 1.

blocks.why: With dependent columns the normal equations stop having one answer. Seeing why is the way into the pseudo-inverse.
blocks.prompt: Same data $b = (1, 2, 6)$, but every $x$ is now 2: $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\1&2\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$. Write $A^\mathsf{T}A$.
hints: Same recipe as before: each entry is (column) · (column).
Row 1, column 2 is $(1,1,1)\cdot(2,2,2)$; row 2, column 2 is $(2,2,2)\cdot(2,2,2)$.

check.say: Symmetric again, and the top-left is still the number of points.

blocks.title: Aᵀb
blocks.why: The other half of the normal equations.
hints: Entry 1 is $(1,1,1)\cdot(1,2,6)$, the same as last time.

check.say: Column 2 is twice column 1, so entry 2 should be twice entry 1.

blocks.title: One equation, twice
blocks.why: Two equations that say the same thing pin down a line, not a point.
blocks.prompt: The normal equations are $3c + 6m = 9$ and $6c + 12m = 18$. Divide each by its first coefficient. Both become $c + k\,m = d$. What are $k$ and $d$?
hints: Now divide $6c + 12m = 18$ by 6, and compare the two.
blocks.solution: Both are $c + 2m = 3$: one equation in two unknowns, so a whole line of solutions.
blocks.next: Test a point on the line

blocks.title: What a point on the line predicts
blocks.why: If two different $(c, m)$ predict the same thing, the data can't tell them apart.
blocks.prompt: Take $p = (c, m) = (1, 1)$, which is on $c + 2m = 3$. What does it predict at each point? Write $Ap$.
hints: Each row of $A$ is $(1, 2)$, so each prediction is $c + 2m$.
All three rows are the same row, so all three predictions are the same number.
blocks.solution: Every point on $c + 2m = 3$ predicts 3 everywhere, because $Ax$ depends only on $c + 2m$.

blocks.title: The residual
blocks.why: Same predictions means the same residual, whichever point on the line you pick.

answer.acceptNote: That is fit − data, the other sign convention: it is $-r$, which is fine.

hints: Data minus prediction, entry by entry.

check.say: Dot $r$ with column 1, $(1, 1, 1)$: it should be 0. Column 2 is twice column 1, so it gives 0 too.

blocks.title: Its score
blocks.why: This is the number that stays fixed along the whole line.

blocks.title: Every point on the line is a best fit
blocks.body: Drag $p$ along the line. Its predictions, its residual and $\|r\|^2 = 14$ never change, while $\|p\|^2$ does. So which best fit should a method return? The next lesson is the task you were last set: the one with the smallest $c^2 + m^2$.
